The process of library cataloguing, often referred to as cataloging, is a meticulous and complex undertaking designed to systematically describe and organize library materials so that they can be easily located by patrons and staff. It begins with the selection of a suitable descriptive format, most commonly the Resource Description and Access (RDA) standard, which provides a structured approach to detailing each item's characteristics. Catalogers then carefully examine the physical item – a book, a journal, a film, or even an audio recording – noting its title, author, publisher, date of publication, and other relevant details. This information is then translated into a machine-readable format, typically using software like Koha or OCLC Connexion, which creates a bibliographic record.  Crucially, catalogers also assign subject headings, using controlled vocabularies such as the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) or the Dewey Decimal System, to indicate the content of the material and facilitate searching.  A unique identifier, the International Standard Serial Number (ISSN) for periodicals or the International Standard Book Number (ISBN) for books, is also assigned to each item. Beyond simply providing factual data, catalogers also craft a concise summary, known as an abstract or description, offering a brief overview of the item’s content and significance to aid the user.  This entire process aims to create a consistent and standardized record, guaranteeing a reliable system for information retrieval within the library.
